en: Oṃ, homage to Śrī Nairātmyā!
To that which they call the Dharmakāya, free from conceptual construction; and the beautiful Saṃbhogakāya, consisting of nothing but incomparable bliss.
May that Blessed One, Vajrasattva, whose emanation body exists for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world, grant you prosperity.

In this single work, we shall set forth, according to our understanding and in accordance with the scriptures, a concise yet extensive proof of selflessness that is clear, explicit, and endowed with insight.

Indeed, the yogi, having seated himself in a comfortable posture in a place conducive to the mind such as a cremation ground, observing the commitments of the five nectars and so forth, free from attachment and fear, with a mind intent on the welfare of sentient beings, should generate the ego-identity of selflessness and meditate on a blue syllable *HŪṂ* upon a sun disk at his heart.

Then, having drawn him forth by means of his own rays illuminating the triple world, [he beholds] the one residing in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, surrounded by eight yoginīs, possessing sixteen arms and eight faces, with a crest fashioned from a garland of skulls, treading upon the four Māras with his four feet, blue in color, and holding in his multitude of right hands the elephant, horse, donkey, bull, camel, human, śarabha, and cat, which are dissolved within the collection of skull-cups.

One should meditate upon him situated in the sky, with his principal face black, his right face as white as the moon or a jasmine flower, his left face intensely red, and his upward-facing face extremely smoky and formidable; his other faces are all dark like bees; he is adorned with a garland of fifty severed heads, his neck is embraced by Nairātmyā, and he holds in his remaining hands the lotus-bowls of Varuṇa, Vāyu, Agni, Rātrinātha (the Moon), Sūrya, Yama, and Dhanada.

Immediately after that, one should worship with the eight yoginīs through the outer and secret reality-worships (*tattvapūjā*). And herein, the worship of Picu-vajra is for the sake of realizing the identity (*tādātmya*) of wisdom and means.

Then, having performed prostrations, the confession of misdeeds, the vow of non-commission of misdeeds, the rejoicing in merit, the dedication of merit, the going for refuge to the Three Jewels, the generation of the bodhicitta, the offering of one’s own body, and the request [to teach], and having cultivated the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras), one should remain in an unestablished form while contemplating the meaning of the mantra that summarizes the essence of the reality of all phenomena: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmakāḥ sarvadharmāḥ*.

Then, recollecting his previous vow, he arises from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), visualizes a sun disk in front of him by means of the syllable *repha* (Ṛ), and within that, visualizes a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) by means of the syllable *hūṃ*. Then, from that crossed-vajra, he should contemplate a vajra-fence, a binding canopy, and below, a ground and a moat consisting of vajras, all produced by masses of rays and vajras radiating forth. Furthermore, by means of the sun and the crossed-vajra, which have become rays and spread out in every direction, he should make all of that firm.

Immediately thereafter, one should visualize within the space-element (khadhātu) the Prajñā in the form of the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), hollow within, exceedingly thick and white, and wide at the top. Then, one should meditate upon a vast eight-petaled lotus of variegated colors situated within that. Then, in its center, one should contemplate a crossed vajra (viśvavajra) produced from the transformation of the syllable *HŪṂ*, which rests in the midst of a solar disc arisen from the letter *Ra*.

In the center of the double-vajra, one should visualize, one above the other, the mandalas of wind, fire, water, and earth—smoky gray, red, white, and green respectively—shaped like a bow, a triangle, a circle, and a square, produced from the transformation of the syllables *yaṃ*, *raṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *laṃ*. Perceiving all this as mere consciousness (*jñānamātra*), one should visualize the palace (*kūṭāgāra*) produced from that [consciousness], which is square, has four doors, is adorned with eight pillars, and is decorated with necklaces and half-necklaces.

Then, one should visualize eight cremation grounds within the enclosure wall. Here, in the east, on a *harītakī* tree, is Devendra, dark blue in color and with the face of an elephant. In the south, on a mango tree, is Yama, white in color and with the face of a buffalo. In the west, on an *aśoka* tree, is Varuṇa, red and with the face of a lion. In the north, on a Bodhi tree, is Kubera, greenish-yellow in hue and with the face of a human.

In the southeast, upon a *karañja* tree, is Vaiśvānara, white in color and goat-faced. In the southwest, upon a *latājaṭī* plant, is Naravāhana, pale yellow and human-faced. In the northwest, upon a *kakubha* tree, is Pavana, yellow and deer-faced. In the northeast, upon a *nyagrodha* tree, is Bhūteśa, variegated and bull-faced. All of these hold a skull-cup in their left hands, have their right hands occupied with various weapons, and display the upper half of their bodies.

Thus, in the eight directions starting from the east, one should visualize, in due order, Ananta, Padma, Vāsuki, Mahāpadma, Takṣaka, Śaṅkhapāla, Karkoṭa, and Kulika. One should also visualize eight clouds of black, white, dark-blue, pale-white, red, yellow, green, and variegated colors. Likewise, the eight guardians of the directions are to be understood as having their well-known colors, and the eight *caityas* are to be understood as having the colors of *yakṣas*.

Then, having visualized a red eight-petaled lotus in the center of the maṇḍala, one should perceive fifteen corpses upon the four petals of that lotus—starting from the east—and likewise in the four corners of the gabled chamber, at the four gates, and below and above. Immediately thereafter, one should meditate on the fifteen vowels beginning with *a*, situated between the moon and sun transformed from the *āli* and *kāli* [vowel and consonant series], mounted upon those corpses. Then, through the transformation of the seed-syllables beginning with *a*, there is a curved knife (*kartikā*) bearing a seed-syllable in every instance.

Then, through the transformation of the moon, sun, and seed-syllable along with the flaying knife (*kartikā*), one should meditate upon the fifteen yoginīs, beginning with Nairātmyā. In this context, the moon possesses the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); the sun possesses the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*); the seed-syllable situated between them is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*); the unification of all these is the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*); and the perfection of the image is the utterly pure sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātu*).

Here, in the center of the hub, one should meditate on Nairātmyā, who arises from the vowel *a*, whose nature is hatred, who is sealed by Akṣobhya, whose essence is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), and whose form is wisdom and method; she embraces the Khaṭvāṅga, which externally represents method, around her neck. On the petals in the east and other directions, one should meditate on Vajrā, Gaurī, Vārī, and Vajraḍākinī, who arise from the vowels *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and *u* respectively; their natures are delusion, malice, passion, and envy; they are sealed by Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi; and their essences are the aggregates of form, sensation, perception, and mental formations.

Then, in the corners of the outer enclosure starting from the northeast, one should visualize Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī, who are produced from the vowels ū, ṛ, ṝ, and ḷ, are sealed by Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, and Amitābha, and have the nature of earth, water, fire, and air.

Thereafter, at the gates in the east and other directions, one should visualize Gaurī, Caurī, Vettālī, and Ghasmarī, who arise from the vowels *ḷ*, *e*, *ai*, and *o*, are sealed by the mudrās of Pukkasī and the others, and have the nature of form, sound, smell, and taste. Immediately after that, below and above, one should visualize Bhūcarī and Khecarī, who arise from the vowels *au* and *aṃ*, whose intrinsic nature is the element of touch and the dharma-element, and whose essence is cyclic existence (*bhava*) and nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, in this context, once the empowerment by their respective family lords (*kuleśa*) has occurred following the generation of the goddesses, their respective family-lord mudrās are to be understood.

These fifteen yoginīs are sixteen years of age, situated within the solar mandala, with a luster like crushed collyrium, having the nature of bodhicitta, with flaming tawny hair standing erect. At their palates they hold four-fingered skull-cups whose nature is Vajrasattva; upon their heads they bear five dry skulls whose nature is the five Buddhas; they have red, round, three-eyed faces with fangs bared in a terrifying mien; they are adorned with garlands of fifteen dry skulls whose nature is the fifteen Mātṛkās; and their waists and hips are draped in tiger skins.
Standing in the *ardhaparyaṅka* dance posture, mounted upon corpses, and bearing the five mudrās;
therein, Akṣobhya is in the form of a wheel, Amitābha is the nature of the earrings, Ratneśa is in the neck-garland, and Vairocana resides in the hand. (1)
Amogha is situated on the belt, and likewise Vajradhṛk is on all the limbs;
the Cakrikā [mudrā] is on the head for bowing to the Guru, the Ācārya, and the chosen deity.
An earring should be worn on the ears so as not to hear ill-spoken words from the Guru or from Vajradhara; a necklace should be worn for the sake of reciting mantras. (3)
Mekhala resolved to adopt the [proper] mudrā; Rucaka resolved to abandon the killing of living beings; and Kṛṣṇāṅga, wearing armlets and anklets, resolved upon a mind of loving-kindness.

The reddish-brown color of the hair is for the purpose of manifesting great passion (*mahārāga*); its upward direction is for the purpose of expressing wrath. Because body, speech, and mind have the nature of supreme passion, the eyes—which possess that same nature—are intensely red. The two arms have the nature of both cyclic existence (*bhava*) and nirvana. The flaying knife is for the purpose of cutting away defects such as pride. The skull-cup, which has three segments and is filled with the blood of the four Māras—the aggregates and so forth—is the embodiment of all conceptual constructions purified through the three realms. It is bent in three places (*tribhaṅga*) due to the purification of the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation bodies.

The slender body [is manifested] through the purity of the svābhāvikakāya. Wearing a tiger skin is to demonstrate the state of being unobstructed. Having one foot placed upon the ground is to demonstrate that there is no objective support (*anālambana*) for the three realms. Having the surface of the earth covered by a single footstep is to demonstrate the state of having a single flavor (*ekarasa*).

Immediately thereafter, rays of light in five forms, emerging from the seed-syllable (*bīja*) residing in the heart, should bring forth the wheel of Nairātmyā, whose nature is the Jñānasattva dwelling in the Akaniṣṭha realm, and cause it to enter the seed-syllable in the heart. Having effected the identity of the Jñānasattva and the Samayasattva, and maintaining the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of being Nairātmyā, one becomes equal to Nairātmyā.
Furthermore, for the purpose of establishing the yoga of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), one should meditate on [the deities] in sequence with the colors black, red, yellow, green, blue, and white.

In that regard, through the process of intensifying meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), first it appears like a full moon shrouded by clouds; then, through further intensification, it appears like an illusion (*māyā*); then, through further intensification, it shines forth like a dream. Immediately thereafter, through the ripening of that intensification, the practitioner of Mahāmudrā attains non-differentiation between the states of dreaming and waking and achieves accomplishment. This is the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

Otherwise, through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, the bodhicitta—which is the nature of great bliss and resides in the midst of the supreme joy—is produced. One should instantly perceive that very [bodhicitta], which consists of fifteen digits (*kalā*), as having the form of the fifteen yoginīs with their previously mentioned colors, symbols, and postures; because it possesses the nature of the five aggregates, the four elements, the six objects, and body, speech, and mind—this is the profound generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
Instantly, without even looking at the seed-syllable, one should perceive the mandala circle consisting of the fifteen yoginīs—this is the completion stage (*utpannakrama*).

Now follows the stage of completion (*pariniṣpannakrama*). Indeed, within the vajra-body, which is empowered by gnosis (*jñāna*), thirty-two channels (*nāḍī*) flow from the place of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). These are the fifteen yoginīs; thus, the body itself consists of the wheel of Nairātmyā. For instance, the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, beginning from the throat and extending to the navel, reside on the left and right sides and are known as the Moon and the Sun. Below the navel, those same two, the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, are the channels of the womb (*yoni-nāḍī*), carrying blood and Akṣobhya respectively.
The *avadhūtī* resides in the middle of the head, throat, heart, navel, and womb, and carries the bodhicitta. These channels are Nairātmyā.

In the indestructible subtle channels located at the head and the crown, respectively carrying the pairs of characteristics of nails and teeth, and hair and body hair, are Vajrā and others. Divyā is in the right ear, carrying skin and impurities; Gaurī is in the spinal column, carrying flesh. Vāmanī and Kūrmajā, located in the left ear and the middle of the eyebrows, carry the chains of sinews and bones; they are Vārī and Bhāvakī. Ḍākinī is located at the base of the eye and the arm, carrying the kidneys and the heart.

Pukkasī resides in the two armpits and breasts, which are filled with impurities and carry bile to the eyes; Mātaṅgī resides in the navel and the tip of the nose, carrying the lungs and the chain of intestines; Caṇḍālī resides in the cold and heat [of the body], located in the mouth and throat, and carries the cords of the flanks and the belly; Pravaṇā resides in the heart, carrying excrement; and Ḍombī resides in the middle of the hair-parting at the genitals, having a joyful countenance.

In the *svarūpiṇī*sāmānya, Gaurī resides in the union of the penis and anus, carrying phlegm (*śleṣman*) and bile (*pitta*). In the state of separation, Hetudāyikā resides in the thighs and shanks, carrying blood (*śoṇita*) and sweat (*sveda*). Caurī resides in the big toe and the back of the foot, carrying fat (*medas*) and tears (*aśru*). Vettālī resides in the big toe and the two knees; therein, the former carries mucus (*kheṭa*) and the latter carries the nasal mucus of a child (*bālasiṃhāṇa*). These two are Ghasmarī.

In the petals of the heart-lotus, starting from the eastern direction and proceeding in order, are Trivṛttā, Kāminī, Gehā, Caṇḍikā, and Māradārikā. Among them, the first pair of channels is Bhūcarī; the remaining ones are Khecarī. Furthermore, whichever channel gives birth to, nourishes, or moves toward a particular [element], it is designated as "flowing that" (tadvahā).

Furthermore, these [deities] possess the nature of the three realms of existence—the body, speech, mind, and enjoyment—and are established within the four wheels (*cakra*) of the body. Among them, the *nirmāṇacakra* (emanation wheel) has sixty-four petals of variegated colors, with the black seed-syllable *a*, and is situated below the navel, facing upward. The *dharmacakra* (dharma wheel) is a white eight-petaled lotus with the black seed-syllable *hūṃ*, situated at the region of the heart. At the throat is the *sambhogacakra* (enjoyment wheel), which has sixteen red petals and the red seed-syllable *praṇava* (*oṃ*).

At the head is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), a white thirty-two-petaled lotus with a downward-facing white seed-syllable *haṃ*, dripping streams of nectar. Here, the distinctions between the moments of bliss (*ānandakṣaṇabheda*) and so forth are to be understood through the oral instructions of the Guru.
The natural sequence (*svābhāvikaḥ kramaḥ*) is the direct realization of the bodhicitta that flows as the non-dual union of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-yuganaddha*).

Then, weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra while maintaining the ego-identity of selflessness (*nairātmyāhaṃkāra*). In this regard, the mantras are the fifteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *svāhā*, which are innate (*sahajasiddha*) and have the nature of the syllable *praṇava*. They are as follows: *oṃ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ svāhā*. Maintaining the ego-identity of red Nairātmyā, one should recite the mantra for agitating the city (*purakṣobhamantra*). In this regard, the mantra is: *oṃ a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa svāhā*.
*Oṃ, the letter *a* is the mouth of all phenomena because they are unarisen from the beginning; oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—this is the *bali* mantra.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ—this is the samaya-adhiṣṭhāna mantra.

Immediately thereafter, at the stage of the direct realization of the maṇḍala-cakra, one should take the two breasts and place the *bola* situated within the *kakkola* of one’s own consort. One should place the bell on both sides.
Having understood the essence of the scriptures of the Mantrayāna with effort from a true guru—
Out of compassion, we have composed this exposition of selflessness.
Alas, how could there be for embodied beings here a definitive realization of the wheel of the mandala of the forest?
[Only] by means of the pollen from the lotus feet of the Lord of the Śabaras...
If there were not the state of having a roughened head.
By whatever merit may be gained through this extensive exposition of the clear realization, may the entire world have its self established in the state of the Vajra-holder.
He whose sorrow and dejection regarding the suffering of the three worlds had been destroyed.
The *Nairātmyāprakāśa* is completed.
